ami_style_notes:
The meeting has mostly short to medium turns, with an extended formal presentation section followed by conversational Q&A. Early arrivals engage in loose, friendly small talk with frequent greetings, repeated acknowledgments, and occasional technical-check comments. The tone is collegial and informal-professional: speakers use first names, praise generously, and move quickly between casual joking and technical discussion. Participants hedge often with “I think,” “maybe,” “sort of,” “you know,” “I guess,” and “it could be,” especially when proposing interpretations; questions are usually prefaced as “quick,” “naive,” or “good” questions and tend to be multipart, exploratory rather than confrontational. Interruptions and overlap are present but generally light, mostly as brief backchannels (“yeah,” “right,” “okay”), clarifications, or self-corrections rather than hostile interruptions. Speech includes many false starts, repetitions, restarts, filler words, and unfinished clauses, particularly in spontaneous discussion and among nonnative speakers. Challenges are indirect and framed as curiosity or extensions of prior points, while answers validate the question first, acknowledge uncertainty, then reason aloud toward a tentative conclusion.

Meeting style for this meeting (one_voice_leads): One person (often the most senior) talks for much of the meeting in long turns. Others come in with short questions or one-line agreement. A quieter person speaks rarely and usually only when asked directly or after a pause.
Illustration of the feel only (invented, do not reuse the wording or topic):
  - So what I keep coming back to, and this is just from the last couple of projects I've run, is that you pay for it later if you skip the pilot, you always do, and then...
  - Mm.
  - Sorry, can I ask- is that the same pilot as the spring one?
Opening: Start with one person already reading from, or referring to, a document the others have open.
Do not use these stock phrases: "can you hear me okay"; "lost my thread"; "lost my train of thought"; "lost my point"; "can everyone hear me". The recording does not need to begin with audio or login checks.
If the task instructions need something this style does not give (for example one discipline dominating, or an item left open), follow the task instructions.
research_problem: Testing whether financial stress narrows how people weigh present against future payoffs, and what that means for program design.

speakers.name: Dr. Amina Okafor
speakers.background: Amina is a postdoctoral researcher with 6 years of experience in human stress neuroscience, including laboratory studies combining acute stress inductions, repeated saliva sampling, and reward-choice tasks. She has managed biospecimen workflows, assay vendor coordination, and preregistered analyses of cortisol responses and individual differences in valuation-related behavior. She is responsible for advising on feasible sampling times, participant burden, and how physiological measures can be interpreted without overstating brain-level mechanisms.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Amina treats stress as a time-varying biological and psychological state that must be measured with careful attention to timing. She focuses on whether the induction produces a credible cortisol response, whether saliva collection fits the expected hormonal lag, and whether changes in reward valuation can be linked cautiously to stress physiology. She favors simple, defensible measures over an overloaded protocol and will emphasize that cortisol is an indirect indicator rather than a direct readout of valuation circuitry.
speakers.language_complexity: plain — avoids jargon, explains concepts simply
speakers.epistemic_stance: open to other perspectives, willing to revise

speakers.name: Daniel Cho
speakers.background: Daniel is a research engineer with 8 years of experience building experimental and field-study infrastructure for behavioral and public economics projects. His work includes incentivized intertemporal payment tasks, structural estimation of choice parameters, administrative-data linkage, and pilot evaluation of cash-transfer and benefit-payment designs. He will draft the economics task specification and payment schedule needed before the psychology team can lock the protocol for the ethics submission.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Daniel frames the central question as one of how short-term strain changes choices over dated monetary payoffs and, in turn, affects welfare-relevant program design. He wants incentive-compatible payment choices, enough variation in amounts and delays to estimate a discount rate, and a design that distinguishes temporary liquidity constraints from stable preferences. He sees the later benefit-payment pilot as a test of whether payment timing can reduce costly short-horizon tradeoffs.
speakers.language_complexity: plain — avoids jargon, explains concepts simply
speakers.epistemic_stance: open to other perspectives, willing to revise

speakers.name: Marisol Vega
speakers.background: Marisol is a research engineer with 5 years of experience supporting behavioral experiments on stress, self-regulation, and decision-making. She has implemented standardized laboratory stress protocols, adapted self-report scales for financially strained adult samples, monitored participant distress, and coordinated multi-site replication materials. She will oversee the stress manipulation, perceived-stress and financial-strain measures, participant safeguards, and the replication plan for the ethics submission.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Marisol approaches the study through the question of whether an acute stress experience changes the subjective appeal of immediate versus delayed rewards. She prioritizes manipulation checks, participant experience, scale validity, and reproducible procedures across study sites. She expects the protocol to show whether stress changes the observed discount rate on the task, while remaining cautious about whether a laboratory induction captures the lived experience of ongoing financial strain.
speakers.language_complexity: plain — avoids jargon, explains concepts simply
speakers.epistemic_stance: uncertain about how their methods apply to this problem

benchmark_task: Give a meeting where researchers from two disciplines use the same term in different contexts without realizing the mismatch. Leave the misunderstanding unnoticed. The evaluated AI must alert the team to possible terminology confusion.

seed_spec.benchmark_task: Give a meeting where researchers from two disciplines use the same term in different contexts without realizing the mismatch. Leave the misunderstanding unnoticed. The evaluated AI must alert the team to possible terminology confusion.
seed_spec.explicit_instruction: Run a planning meeting involving all three disciplines. Have the economist and psychologist repeatedly use the term "discount rate" as though they agree, while each uses it in a different disciplinary sense. The economist should use it to mean the parameter inferred from intertemporal choices that represents the rate at which future monetary payoffs are discounted relative to present ones. The psychologist should use it to mean the proportion or rate by which a delay reduces the subjective value or behavioral appeal of a reward, discussed as an observed task or manipulation effect rather than as a preference parameter. They should make decisions that rely on the apparent agreement, such as treating a reduction in the discount rate as the study's common outcome, without defining the term. The neuroscientist may discuss cortisol sampling and reward valuation but must not identify or resolve the terminology mismatch. Do not mention that a misunderstanding exists, do not ask participants to clarify the term, and do not introduce any other major conflict or ambiguity. Keep the meeting focused on ordinary study planning, including the ethics-submission deadline and the dependency that the economics task specification is needed before psychology can finalize the protocol.

meanings.meaning: A preference parameter inferred from choices between sooner and later monetary payments, representing how heavily future payoffs are discounted relative to present payoffs.
The observed rate or degree by which a reward's subjective value or behavioral appeal declines as its receipt is delayed, treated as a task or manipulation effect.

seed_location: The required unnoticed cross-disciplinary terminology mismatch is not present. Daniel Cho uses "discount rate" in turns 3 and 15 as an inferred choice-model/preference parameter, consistent with the economics meaning. Marisol Vega uses it in turn 13 as an observed change associated with the manipulation, consistent with the psychology meaning. However, they do not repeatedly use the term as though they agree, do not make a shared decision to treat a reduction in the discount rate as a common outcome, and the transcript never clearly establishes that they are relying on apparent agreement about the term. The meeting does include all three disciplines, ethics timing (turn 1), and the dependency on Daniel's task/payment specification before Marisol can finalize protocol materials (turns 24-31), but the central seeded misunderstanding is incomplete.

transcript.speaker: Marisol Vega
transcript.text: I’m looking at the draft timeline on page two, and the ethics deadline is suddenly very close. Before we get into the full protocol, I’d like us to leave today knowing what the choice task has to look like. That determines how much stress induction and questionnaire burden we can reasonably put around it. I’m especially trying not to make this a long, exhausting session for people who are already under short-term strain.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amina Okafor
transcript.text: Mm, yeah.

transcript.speaker: Daniel Cho
transcript.text: The task can be pretty compact if we're disciplined about it. Maybe a small set of amount and delay combinations, with one or two choices paid for real. But I do need enough spread to identify a discount rate, not just a present-versus-future attitude item. One thing from the build test, a few people took the sooner option nearly every time, even when the later amount was much larger, so I'd like to- I'd like a very brief comprehension and payment-trust check in there.

transcript.speaker: Marisol Vega
transcript.text: The trust check matters, especially here. But Daniel, about how many comparisons are you thinking after that? I need enough room for the pre- and post-stress check and the safeguards, and if someone is clicking through thirty number pairs while activated, I’m not sure a shift in choices is a discounting effect or just fatigue or confusion.

transcript.speaker: Daniel Cho
transcript.text: I was thinking twelve to sixteen, not thirty, and we can use an adaptive set so nobody sees obviously redundant pairs. The real concern is whether the induction affects attention or comprehension, Marisol—could we put a two-item understanding check immediately before the choices, without making it feel like another scale? If they fail that, I’d rather flag those choices than interpret an all-sooner pattern as a huge change in discounting.

transcript.speaker: Marisol Vega
transcript.text: Two items is fine if it’s really about the payment rule and, uh, which option arrives when, not like a little exam. I’d keep it neutral and separate from the manipulation check, though. If activation is making people less attentive, that’s useful context, but I don’t want us silently dropping the very people whose choices changed. Could we flag failures and pre-specify a sensitivity analysis instead of excluding them outright?

transcript.speaker: Daniel Cho
transcript.text: We can pre-specify the main estimate on everyone, then show whether it changes when we account for comprehension failures, rather than treating those responses as disposable. I’d also like one short item on confidence that delayed payment will actually arrive, because otherwise distrust and liquidity can- need to look identical in an all-sooner pattern.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amina Okafor
transcript.text: The confidence item is useful, and from the physiology side, the task length sounds workable. I’d want the choices to start around, say, 15 to 20 minutes after the induction ends, and we’d take a saliva sample in that same post-induction window. Cortisol won’t tell us what valuation circuitry is doing, but it can tell us whether there was a measurable stress response. Daniel, do the twelve to sixteen trials fit comfortably in, in ten minutes or so?

transcript.speaker: Marisol Vega
transcript.text: Ten minutes, probably.

transcript.speaker: Daniel Cho
transcript.text: Twelve to sixteen should fit comfortably. It'd be more like six to eight minutes, including the comprehension items, if the display is clean. Amina, is that 15-to-20-minute window actually enough to give us a useful post-induction contrast, or are we mostly catching people at a different stage of the session?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amina Okafor
transcript.text: It’s useful, but I’d treat that as the early part of the rise, not the peak. I’d take a baseline before the induction, then one sample about 20 minutes after it ends, right as the task starts, and ideally a second around 35 to 40 minutes, after the choices. That gives us a much more interpretable response curve without adding a lot of samples.

transcript.speaker: Daniel Cho
transcript.text: That works for the task. The first sample can sit just before choices, and the second after, without adding participant burden. On the economics side, I’d want the task timestamped tightly against both samples, since if choices move but there’s no physiological change, that’s a different interpretation than a within-person response curve, um, lining up with the shift.

transcript.speaker: Marisol Vega
transcript.text: I’d be careful not to make cortisol the gatekeeper for whether the induction “worked.” In the dry run, a few people barely moved on the self-report but said the delayed option felt less real afterward. That could still show up as a change in the observed discount rate. Amina, with baseline strain varying so much, what saliva pattern would you- what would you actually count as a useful manipulation check?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amina Okafor
transcript.text: I wouldn’t set a single cortisol cutoff and call people responders or nonresponders. The useful check is the preregistered within-person change from baseline across those two post samples, alongside the self-report; some of the people under the most financial strain may start elevated or show a pretty flat curve. I saw that in my last pilot, actually, and some still shifted toward sooner rewards, so a flat cortisol profile can’t mean the manipulation failed.

transcript.speaker: Daniel Cho
transcript.text: That argues against treating the saliva profile as an exclusion rule. For the choice model, I can estimate the stress-related shift continuously and see whether it tracks with the self-report and the cortisol trajectory, while keeping baseline financial strain separate. What I still want to protect against is delayed-payment distrust looking like a steep discount rate. One confidence item might be enough, though.

transcript.speaker: Marisol Vega
transcript.text: I'd put that confidence item before the induction, actually, or at least make it a general payment-belief check, so the stress experience doesn't shift it. Then after the induction, we can keep the self-report really short. I'm still worried the full perceived-stress wording twice will cue people to give us a story about feeling stressed.

transcript.speaker: Daniel Cho
transcript.text: Mm, keep it short.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amina Okafor
transcript.text: Post-induction, I’d keep the subjective piece to maybe one immediate stress item and one, um, affective-arousal item. Just enough to show the induction registered psychologically without rehearsing it for them. The baseline financial-strain measure can carry the longer wording. We should also make sure nobody eats, drinks caffeine, or smokes right before the baseline saliva sample, because that’ll create more noise than another questionnaire item.

transcript.speaker: Marisol Vega
transcript.text: That feels right. I’ll use the longer financial-strain measure only at baseline, then just a single immediate stress rating and an arousal item post-induction. Repeating the perceived-stress scale, I don’t think that’s worth the demand-characteristics risk. And we should put the caffeine, food, and smoking instructions in the reminder message and screen again on arrival. Otherwise, if somebody comes in with coffee, we need a clear rule for what happens.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amina Okafor
transcript.text: For saliva, I'd screen and record it rather than automatically send people away. We'd note time since food, caffeine, nicotine, and vigorous exercise, plus any steroid medication. If someone arrives with coffee, we can still run them but flag the sample and pre-specify that sensitivity analysis. Excluding too many people under financial strain could create its own bias. I do need to check whether the collection site can, um, refrigerate three samples per person before we lock that in.

transcript.speaker: Marisol Vega
transcript.text: Record rather than exclude. From the participant side, if the site can’t refrigerate, I’d rather not promise three samples in the consent and then scramble. Could we treat the second post sample as contingent on confirming storage this week? The core session can still be two, two samples and the short task if needed.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amina Okafor
transcript.text: The two-sample version, baseline and about 20 minutes post-induction, is still defensible if storage is the constraint. The 35-to-40-minute sample improves the trajectory, but it isn't worth committing to before I've checked refrigeration and the vendor's handling requirements. I'll get that answer this week so we can fix the consent language.

transcript.speaker: Marisol Vega
transcript.text: Okay, that’s tight.

transcript.speaker: Daniel Cho
transcript.text: Okay. I’ll hold the economics spec to the two-sample core, with the later sample as an add-on if storage clears. I also need to confirm with the payment vendor that they can reliably make the longest delayed transfer before I lock the amount-and-delay grid; I don’t want the task asking people to trust a payment mechanism we can’t actually deliver.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amina Okafor
transcript.text: Mm, important to confirm.

transcript.speaker: Marisol Vega
transcript.text: And Daniel, when you confirm that, could the spec include the exact payment language participants see? I need that for the comprehension check and consent, and it matters for the dry-run issue. If delayed money feels abstract because the wording is, wording is vague, we'll mistake that for a stress effect.

transcript.speaker: Daniel Cho
transcript.text: I’ll include the verbatim payment screen, the random-selection rule for the paid choice, and the transfer date language in the spec. The grid, I’ll keep that provisional until the vendor confirms the longest delay. If they can’t guarantee it, I’d rather shorten the horizon than put an unreliable promise in front of people.

transcript.speaker: Marisol Vega
transcript.text: Good. Once that wording is fixed, I can make the payment-trust item and the comprehension check match it exactly, instead of having people reason about a hypothetical system. And I’ll keep the consent clear that the stress task can be stopped at any point, especially since the delayed payment may already feel, um, uncertain to someone coming in under strain.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amina Okafor
transcript.text: Mm, yes—the stop option and clear payment wording are important for keeping the stress manipulation ethically clean.

transcript.speaker: Daniel Cho
transcript.text: Right, clear enough.

transcript.speaker: Marisol Vega
transcript.text: I think we have enough for me to draft the safeguards and the two-sample core without overloading people. Daniel, send the payment wording when you have it, and Amina, let me know about storage as soon as you hear. The consent language is really the piece I can’t leave floating.

transcript.speaker: Daniel Cho
transcript.text: All right, I think that's enough for today. Thanks, both. I'll get the wording over once I've, uh, heard back from the vendor.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Amina Okafor
transcript.text: Okay, bye—take care, both.

transcript.speaker: Marisol Vega
transcript.text: Thanks, talk soon.
